domain: Whether translation between languages is fundamentally a creative act or a mechanical one, and what changes when we admit it is creative
topic: Whether translation between languages is fundamentally a creative act or a mechanical one, and what changes when we admit it is creative

movement.gist: Author opens scornful of the romantic cliché that 'translation is impossible' and 'something is always lost' — dismisses it as sentimental cover for sloppy work, insists a good translator simply gets the words right.

Concedes, against will, that word-for-word rendering repeatedly fails on real examples (idiom, rhythm, connotation) — forcing the admission that choices must be made, i.e. that some interpretive judgment is unavoidable. Plants the decoy thesis: translation requires skilled compromise, but is still fundamentally a technical craft of approximation.

Pushes further under the weight of evidence (great translations that outlive their originals in the receiving language, translators whose versions are studied as literature in their own right) to concede something larger: the translator isn't approximating a fixed original but producing a new verbal artifact that has its own aesthetic life. This displaces the decoy — the real thesis emerges: translation is authorship, not approximation.

Affirms the conversion — translation is creative authorship — but prices it: this means the translator's name should carry as much responsibility and credit as the original author's, and readers must give up the comforting fiction of unmediated access to foreign literature.

primary.axis: translation as faithful transcription vs. translation as authorship
poles: the translator as an invisible, exact conduit
the translator as a co-author who necessarily rewrites

secondary.axis: the value of fidelity vs. the value of felt experience for the reader
poles: fidelity to the original's exact words
fidelity to the original's effect on a reader

tension_system.interaction: the secondary tension starts as a side-argument for accuracy but ends up supplying the real thesis: that what's lost is not accuracy but the translator's own authorship being erased even as it is exercised

family_realization.note: Author opens skeptical ('never trusted'), reluctantly concedes untranslatability ('concede this, reluctantly'), admits craft model 'collapses,' ends accepting authorship as 'price.' Each step prices cost.

ending_behavior.note: 'The name on the spine'—filed as 'trivial'—becomes the invoice due, displacing craft technicality. Final stance: resolution costed (reader's comfort revoked, translator's liability made visible).

voice_consistency.note: Consistent etymological archaeology: *translatus* from *transferre*, *auctor* from *augere*. Mostly resists generic cadence, though 'invoice falls due' edges toward personification.

distractor_efficiency.note: Q1(A): stage_misattribution catches paragraph-two concession-as-thesis. Q3(B): stance_misread inverts the illusion claim. Q5(A): causal_inversion tempts (structural vs. motive). Solid traps.

explanation_quality.note: Each elimination ties to passage locations ('technician's model collapses,' 'invoice falls due,' 'auctor from augere'). Mechanisms named: zero-sum false_symmetry, causal_inversion, stage_misattribution—precise.

answers.reasoning: Passage moves from craft view to authorship thesis and its naming consequence.
Unstated premise: tradition-building/imitation constitutes origination, not mere approximation.
Final paragraph explicitly reveals the 'trivial' naming issue as the costly real payload.
Assumption: origination anywhere entails authorial credit and liability, per auctor argument.
Illusion of unmediated Tolstoy depended on translator's authorship being unseen.
Author starts skeptical, concedes evidence, follows argument to uncomfortable authorship conclusion.
